utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mr. Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. For General Hadzihasanovic, Ms. Edina Residovic, Muriel Cauvin, Mirna Milanovic Lalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to welcome everyone to the courtroom which is very cozy since we are very close to each other. Mr. Registrar, you have made some changes and could you inform us of these changes in relation to the transcript from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Unfortunately we finished quite late yesterday and the work was still in progress. I'm still verifying everything. With your leave I can clarify these points after the second break. I think that the transcript will be changed in accordance with the information that I provided to the interpreters last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll see about that after the second break. Mr. Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I hope you can hear us. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Without wasting anymore time, let the Defence take the floor to continue with their examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Siljak. Yesterday you indicated on the map -- you drew the positions where the BH army were located as well as the forces of the Republika Srpska and HVO units. I will now move on to a series of questions that concern the relationship between the 306th Brigade and the BH Army in the territory where your brigade was present. And I will also ask some questions that have to do with the clashes between these units. My first question is as follows: When you indicated the location of the various units, you also indicated the road linking up this area with Travnik and Zenica. Could you please tell me, Mr. Siljak, what sort of a road is it, what importance does it have to the population, and in particular does it have any importance for the BH determine -- did it have any importance for the BH army and your brigade?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road links up Zenica via Guca Gora, Han Bila, and Ovnak with Travnik. The main road linking Zenica and Travnik was a highway to Lasva and from Lasva to Zenica. But for the most part of that period it was not passable, not because it wasn't in good repair but because there were HVO checkpoints, and in particular there was a checkpoint at Okuka, the crossroads for Novi Travnik. For this reason the road was not used, or rather, army members found it very difficult to use it. The other road that linked Zenica and Travnik was again a main road and it turned off from other roads from Vjetrenice to Zenica. And for similar reasons, for the same reasons, the army of the BH republic didn't use this road to a great extent. The road from Guca Gora connected Travnik with the Bila Valley, or rather connected Bila Valley with Zenica, and Zenica and Travnik. Since initially the 306th Brigade, when it was being established, relied on the municipal defence staff in Travnik which was already in operation, this was a road used for supplies by this unit. This was a road that I used and the commander used to go to work. It was a transit road used by thousands of people, by refugees, by the population moving from Travnik to Zenica and the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: The units that were based in that area, for example those of the 312th and the 314th, et cetera, in what way could these units reach the combat positions facing the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 314th Motorised Brigade was located in Zenica, but its positions were in the territory of the municipality of Travnik. Positions facing the Serbian/Montenegrin aggressor in the wider region of Meokinje. And when going to those positions, they had to leave Zenica, go via Ovnak as far as Han Bila, and then continue through Mehurici, Pula, Bukovica, to reach the position at Meokinje. It's a HVO checkpoint established at Ovnak, permanently there, regardless of the discussions and the negotiations. It was never possible to take joint action to remove the checkpoints because there were agreements on both sides. And later on the joint command tried to reach agreements to remove all checkpoints. However, that checkpoint was never removed and I know units going towards the positions facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor were returned from that checkpoint. Similarly, from Zenica -- the 7th Muslim Brigade would go to positions in the Travnik municipality. This road went through Ovnak, Han Bila, Guca Gora, in the direction of Travnik. And members of the 7th Muslim Brigade also had problems at that checkpoint. Because sometimes not even authorisation from the superior commander of the HVO was accepted. At that checkpoint they would stop men, maltreat them and send them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, since you were the chief of staff of the 306th Brigade, could you tell me where the -- in that area there was an HVO Brigade, and if so, what was the name of the brigade and tell me what sort of relationships were there between your units, or rather at any point in time did those relationships deteriorate and lead to a conflict.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially when the 306th Brigade was being formed in the area from which men were taken into the 306th, there was an HVO Brigade, a Travnik HVO Brigade. At the beginning of April it had its headquarters in Guca Gora and an HVO Brigade was formed. It was called the Frankopan Brigade. Its headquarters were located in Guca Gora and it had its units in Cukle, Grahovcici, in Maline, in Guca Gora, so in that wider area in the Bila Valley, in villages inhabited by Croats. In the first stage initially, the relationship between the commands of both brigades was influenced by a number of factors, by numerous factors, for example the situation in other areas, in the territory of adjacent municipalities. And while the 306th Brigade was being formed, there were problems in Novi Travnik which had a direct effect on the situation in the Bila Valley. I know when I arrived there that the HVO established some sort of lines facing the villages with Muslim inhabitants around the Guca Gora, Maline, Radonjici, Mala Bukovica, in that area; and on the other side you Sarici and Banovici. In January 1993 there were conflicts, clashes, again incidents in other municipalities and once more this had an effect on our territory. Certain elevated positions were taken. More checkpoints were set up on that road to control the passage of people and vehicles. You couldn't move freely without authorisations, or rather, if you tried to use these roads there were problems. So I must say that this provoked a reaction in Bosniak villages, too. As I indicated on the map - I showed you where these villages were - in Guca Gora, at the entrance to and exit from Guca Gora there was an HVO checkpoint. And similarly, at the beginning of the road to Maline at the entrance the Bosniak population for security purposes - it's not as there were -- there had been some sort of army order - but for security purposes they set up checkpoints on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the blockade of roads and the impossibility of troops, to refuse them [as interpreted] to reach combat positions, did this have an effect on the chain of command itself? Where was the command of your brigade deployed?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I drew the location of the command post of the brigade on the map. It was on the premises in the facilities of the Bila mine, a place inhabited by Croats. The village of Baje which is in the vicinity of the command and of the main office of the Bila mine. There were Croats there. I don't know how I would put this. But if it was our intention to remain there and not to be afraid and to fight the enemy together, at that moment we thought about the command post, not about the HVO and the Croats as enemies. Otherwise we would probably have located the command post somewhere else. But in view of the situation in the field, the Bila Valley was divided into a number of regions. It was impossible to pass through. The region from which men entered the 306th Brigade was no longer one single entity. It consisted of enclaves and it was impossible to pass from one enclave to another. As a result, it was impossible to reach the command post and likewise it was impossible for the units to carry out the tasks as they had been ordered. They couldn't carry out the tasks against the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor so that officers from the brigade command were separated from the command. And at one point in time they were present at six locations. And I'm referring to the officers of the brigade command. This was just before the conflict broke out and at a time when it was not possible to move around freely in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Siljak. Tell me, because of the tension that developed, did the HVO at any point in time attack the BH army and did such excesses lead to the death of individuals? And if so, what was the relationship between the 306th and the -- what was the attitude of the 306th and the BH army as far as avoiding a conflict with the HVO is concerned?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first excesses in our territory which resulted in death, it was the death and the killing of a civilian on the 15th of April, 1993, the day of the army. Dautovic Sakib was killed by a sniper bullet on the 15th of April. As soon as such an incident, this results in excessive behaviour, tension, checkpoints set up, and individuals are maltreated. There were numerous reports about how people had been stopped at HVO checkpoints, things -- items had been confiscated from civilians or from the soldiers. And an open attack was launched by the HVO against the command post of the 306th Brigade. And again, this resulted in death and two members of the military police were wounded. Then there were reports on HVO activity in Kljaci, Alihodze, Zukici, Karahodze, and such reports were almost daily. And again HVO activity resulted in death. There was a lot of sniper activity that resulted in death. I tried to show you where the village of Ricice was located and Brankovac. There were cries were help because they were surrounded. They weren't allowed to leave their houses. They were being threatened. There were cries from Velika Bukovica as well, cries of help as this village was surrounded too. And the village of Radojcici towards the end of May was also attacked and artillery and infantry weapons were used to attack this village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, I will now ask you to have a look at the documents that you saw yesterday. I will ask these documents to be shown you. And in relation to what you were just saying, could you please have a look at the part entitled: "Relation with the HVO." Have a look at items 1 to 17. And could you then tell me whether you recognise these documents as documents that come from the 306th Brigade, or rather documents forwarded to the command of the 306th Brigade. And once you have had a look at these documents, I will put a series of questions to you about them. Have you managed to have a look at all the documents?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at document number 12. I've had a look at the documents. I recognise them on the whole, these documents. Reports on operative events made by the operations and instruction organ of the brigade, and they were referred directly to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document 0674. It's under number 1 before you. Please tell me since you mentioned incidents, HVO attacks and attacks that resulted in death and you also mentioned an attack against the command, tell me what sort of measures the 306th took in accordance with orders from the command and the supreme command staff. Did you respond to these conflicts or did you react in some other way?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see in this document, the 306th command carried out the orders of its superior command and attempted to resolve conflictual [as interpreted] situations and avoid conflict. And they used all their means to do so. You can see that the most responsible officers from the brigade command were engaged in this task. They were to inform the men and request that this order was implemented. They say that the command of the 306th, the chief of staff, and the assistant for operations and training will visit the field in order to implement the order. And since at this time there were problems at the line towards the Serbian/Montenegrin aggressor, not just because he was attacking but because there were excesses in the Bila Valley where soldiers' families who were at positions facing the Serbian aggressor, as a result the chief of staff had to go to the forward command post to explain the situation. That was his task. And he was to do this to prevent further escalations, or rather to resolve the problem in a peaceful manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 3. This is Defence number 0797. Does this document refer to some of the numerous situations that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that there were many such situations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. resulting in death. This is a document that refers to these situations. But the date, the number on the document is wrong. But this was on the 28th of May just before the conflict, almost immediately before the open conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at document number 4. Is this another document that refers to HVO attacks and excesses in relation to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document it says that the relation was tense, that there were incidents. But similarly the document shows that we had problems as far as communications with our superior command is concerned because in the 306th Brigade we often had problems as far as communications with the command and the OG Zapad is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you a document from February and you assessed the sort of equipment you had on that occasion. If you look at item 2, "Our own forces," paragraph 2. Could you please tell me whether the level of supply in your brigade -- and did it -- did the level of supply improve or was it worse than the situation the brigade was in in February as a result of the fact that you were surrounded by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We hoped for a better situation, but here it says that the situation was deteriorating. As far as the reserves were concerned, they were disappearing and it was impossible for us to obtain new supplies since the territory was under a blockade and it was impossible to get in contact or to reach our superior commands to resupply ourselves. When we tried to do this, to reach them we would be stopped at checkpoints and vehicles would be confiscated. Members of the brigade command and other people from the brigade would suffer this fate when they tried to carry out such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document under number 5.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report of the intelligence organ, that is the assistant of chief of staff, my own assistant in the 306th Brigade. He made an assessment of HVO forces after the establishment of the Frankopan Brigade. From this document you can see the deployment of the Frankopan Brigade in this territory, the same thing that I tried to explain using that map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this document there is reference to the taking of land features. Does this document reflect what you testified to yesterday, namely that the HVO was encircling BH army positions and capturing dominant features in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is very eloquent. I'm sorry that I cannot show it to you on the relief map because the HVO captured all the dominant land features, the pass between Zenica and Travnik, then a valley where Han Bila, a Muslim village, was. Then again when you go towards Travnik, the next pass is Trava [phoen]. That's where Guca Gora is. It goes on towards Vlasic and Hum and towards Greba and Pokrajcici. On the south side there is Mosor village, Radojcici village in the same valley, and then again there is another pass called Postinje which leads to the Bukovica feature, the last pass, the last ridge, on that path. So they controlled all these passes, ridges, and land features, and they actually did not allow any communication without their express authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document 6, paragraph 3 entitled "HVO" and tell me: Does this report which you submitted to the command of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Group West, which was your direct superior, reflect exactly what you've been saying about the establishment of checkpoints and the conduct of HVO personnel at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The checkpoints are indicated here. However, at this juncture I would like to say something about one thing in which I had a direct role. It says: One unit concerning 22 HVO soldiers was disarmed. They were returning from the position in Turbe. The arms taken away from them were duly returned with the presence of UNPROFOR personnel. I'm saying this because the order from our superior command was to avoid conflict by all means, to always try to deal with situations peacefully. And this particular incident happened when I got an assignment to go to that checkpoint and diffuse the tension. It was not easy, however, to resolve this problem was there was no real command in that time. It was more persuasion than command. And I did my best to persuade them to return the weapons because our main objective was to deal with everything peacefully and go forward together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document 8 now, the part relating to the relations with the HVO. It's dated 6th May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that incidents were a daily occurrence, and again, this document reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document 9 dated the 7th May. Are you aware of this event?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, because they came back. They were unable to cross the checkpoint on the way to Onaka [phoen] and our physical liaison with the corps command was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the next document which is number 10, 9th May.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a report reflecting the knowledge we were gaining about HVO activities. HVO continued to confiscate various vehicles including the vehicle belonging to the Bila mine. It is just one among many documents of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document dated 12th May.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this document continues to speak of the same thing as the previous one. Checkpoint activity, shootings, confiscation of weapons, foodstuffs, vehicles. In this case it was Lukovic Edhem -- a civilian, not a member of the 306th Brigade -- who had his property confiscated. But also in the Konjska area two rifles were taken away. Konjska is close to Velika and Mala Bukovica, around Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, in keeping with the regulations of the army under attack from the enemy, the army has the right to respond in the same way. You say that you were avoiding to respond and you tried to dissolve tensions. After this event you were reporting does this document testify to your efforts to not respond in the same way and to resolve the situation peacefully?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. In the Bila mine near the command post when the joint command staff came, including representatives of the HVO, representatives of the international forces, and the UNPROFOR, our signalsman was killed and we continued negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day a meeting was scheduled at the joint command. HVO representatives, international observers, UNPROFOR representatives, the Frankopan Brigade, and the 306th Brigade. At the command post of the 306th Brigade near the Bila mine, as the HVO was arriving fire was opened from a nearby position, even at UNPROFOR APCs. And on that occasion one of the signalsmen of the 306th Brigade was killed. We did not use this as an excuse to stop the negotiations; on the contrary, we continued the talks. And I remember after that meeting I wrote an order to my subordinate units that objectives and agreements reached at that meeting should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please now look at documents 12, 13, and 14, and please tell us what are they reporting on. Which event?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not directly involved in this event, but it was awful to hear members of our brigade as they were reporting on it. A part of the superior officers of the brigade command left for Mehurici on leave. In Baje village they were stopped by HVO personnel at a checkpoint, disarmed them, took away various items including their clothing, such as vests, and they made them graze, eat grass.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any specific members of the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the security assistant Delalic, Halim Husic, assistant for morale, because they reported later, as direct participants, to the commander. They were assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you respond in a military way, by military action, to such provocation or did you try to prevent a conflict?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We addressed the protests to the Frankopan Brigade because we had daily communications with them. A mixed operations team had been established that was supposed to deal with incidents on the ground. And in that operations team there were two representatives of the 306th Brigade and two representatives of the Frankopan Brigade. And we tried to deal with clashes through that forum, through that team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document number 15.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another document speaking to the activity of HVO from these elevations that were developed by engineers for action from the environs and it also speaks about the problems we had in this Ricice village, because there were constant cries for help from the population. In Nova Bila there were some Bosniak families. In Stara Bila, there were very few, but still there were some. And they started to come and to complain that they were being driven out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly look at document 16 now and tell me if you recognise it or you recognise maybe the signature.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the signature because I wrote this paper myself. And the document, as I was saying now, is the order that I wrote after the killing of our signalsman after fire was opened at UNPROFOR APCs. And let me say in passing that men from the UNPROFOR APC returned fire to the HVO, whereupon the HVO stopped firing. This document was issued after the joint meeting. It reflects the discussion at the meeting and everything that was agreed, including the measures that need to be taken to implement the conclusions of the meeting. If you read this paper, you will really see that the intention behind it is good, that we were trying to resolve all our mutual clashes in order to be flee to deal with our common enemy. And the objective of the command and battalion commanders is to realise this on the ground. It was only possible to implement this if you go to the ground and persuade the troops on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I wanted to clarify, namely your relations with the HVO on the eve of the June conflict. Tell me now, what happened in end May and early June. Did the army attack Croatian villages in your area?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said how the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I have been very patient with my colleague, but I think it's public knowledge that there was several armies in that area. So when she says: "Did the army attack Croatian villages in your area," I mean I think she needs to be a little more specific because she keeps leading him on and providing him with the information and then he gives the answer to suit. I don't think...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the BH army and its units, specifically the 306th Brigade where you were chief of staff, to the best of your knowledge attack Croatian territories, Croatian villages, organising heavy attacks on these villages?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to answer this question I have to describe the situation before the all-out conflict on the 8th of June. You saw from this document that Ricice village and another village were encircled and the population wanted this situation resolved. Local people of military age from these villages were members of our brigade and we felt responsibility for their families. Also in the area of Velika Bukovica we had the same situation. That village was completely encircled by the HVO and they were crying for help, too. Furthermore, from Travnik in early June, I'm not sure, it could have been the 3rd of June, we started hearing shooting. It seemed to be an open conflict, clash. We had no information what was going on exactly, but there was shooting. At that time in the Lasva Valley and in the area around Travnik there were clashes. And I have to describe to you the situation in which the 306th Brigade found itself, along with the command, to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me that I skipped one question. In view of this dramatic situation that you have been describing so calmly before the Trial Chamber, although it must have been a real drama in your life, I have to ask you, in May, after all those reports that you wrote did the command of the 3rd Corps react by issuing an order instructing the brigades how to act? And did you take any measures to implement that order?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to add that in the Travnik municipality in order to diffuse the tensions and find a peaceful solution, a joint command of the BH army and HVO was established. And they tried to calm the situation on the ground. So all the protests that we made and addressed to the HVO and any complaints they had about the BH army conduct were dealt by this joint command in Travnik [as interpreted]. I don't know, but I think it's important that I took part in one of those last meetings when the joint command dealt with the situation in the Bila region. To prevent the conflict a meeting was scheduled on the 30th of May in Guca Gora and it was supposed to be attended by international representatives, observers, the UNPROFOR, the commanders of the 306th and the Frankopan Brigades, et cetera. At the time, a presidency of the Travnik municipality was formed in Bila with the representation of both Bosniaks and Croats. So both the military and politicians were represented in this body and they were able to negotiate and try to find a peaceful solution. I came to attend that meeting on an UNPROFOR APC because I was unable to return to the brigade command because the territory was under blockade. On the 27th when I was taking that computer to Travnik, it was taken away from me. So I came to attend that meeting. It was fruitless in the end. And when it was over, since I was one of those participants what couldn't play an active role, I asked a former schoolmate of mine who was representing the Frankopan brigade, Franjo Lujanovic. We were in sixth grade together, we went to the teachers college together. I addressed him and said: On behalf of the army I am prepared to inspect the positions of the BH army and the HVO army together with you and to implement on the ground what we just agreed today. I said that to Franjo Lujanovic, my colleague. In fact, I said I trust Franjo Lujanovic, my former schoolmate and friend. Let the two of us go together and do it. Franjo Lujanovic's superiors said, I cannot make the promises that you are making because I don't have the mandate -- although he didn't use the word "mandate," he said something to that effect. So that meeting was interrupted and we went to have lunch together. And the meeting did not have any particular results. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, as to your question if we received orders from the superior command with regard to this particular situation --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all I would like you to look at an exhibit document listed under number 1. It's a Prosecution exhibit, number 418. Please have a look and tell us whether you recognise the document and the signature, and only in that light would you please answer the previous question.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an emergency report about the implementation of our assignment of the 19th of May. It's an interim report, rather. I wrote it in longhand because we only had one typewriter for the whole brigade and not everything could be typed. This report was drawn up under the order of the command of the 3rd Corps of the 18th of May. On the 18th of May, we received an order to make an assessment of the situation because there were developments on the ground involving constant incidents. Also at the time we had knowledge from intelligence organs that there were contacts between HVO and the Serb side in the Vjetrenice region. Representatives of the HVO and the Serb side were holding meetings and going back to their units. This seemed very strange to us, of course, and we got an order from superior command to make a plan for a deployment of forces only in case that our unit is attacked. So it was not an offensive plan. It was a plan to respond to an attack from the Serb side with the HVO uninvolved; second variety of the plan, attack by HVO without the Serb side; and the worst possibility, a joint attack of the HVO on the Serb side against the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please pick up with you left off before. You had this meeting in Guca Gora with all these representatives that was fruitless. Tell me, at this point where was the brigade command, where were you the commander, and what were the events following up to the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said we went -- all of us who attended that meeting -- to Krpeljici to have lunch, both Bosniaks and Croats. In Krpeljici we continued to talk about the problems, about the fact that we should find a solution. And that's how we parted that day. It's unbelievable but it's true that there were only a few people left at the command post in Rudnik. There was no way somebody could reach them, replace them, or help them. I found there the assistant commander of the brigade, assistant commander for materiel and supply, and the assistant commander for moral and religious affairs. Only these three or four assistant commanders were there. A part of the brigade command was stuck in the villages where they happened to be. In Kljaci there were three or four. In Karahodze the same thing. In Han Bila there were individual members of the brigade command, in Han Bila as well. And part of the brigade command happened to be in Mehurici. And they were unable to go anywhere, to leave. So it was our task to help the defence of these villages in keeping with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, just show us on the map in which places you had parts of your brigade command so that we can understand it better. Even I who know the territory find it difficult to follow when it's not accompanied by visual aid.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer a clear map without any markings so that I can show you the territory and how it was divided, including the spots where the 306th Brigade was then as a unit and where the individual members of the command were stuck. This is the Bila mine. This is Krpeljici, where I was with the commander of the brigade and those two assistant commanders. In the Mosor village there was one member of the brigade command. In Mehurici, which is the command post of the 1st Battalion, there was also another part of the brigade command. Men who actually resided in this area which is exclusively Bosniak. Podovi village, or as we call it, Pode. There was one member of the brigade command. In Han Bila there were two members of the brigade command. In Kljaci village, there were two or three members of the brigade command -- so that the command of the brigade was scattered all over the place. In this territory -- you see this mine that I encircled was -- contained part of the brigade command that had had no communications with anyone else. Why? Because this road from Sarici went down towards the Bila Valley and further on towards Baje and Grahovcici. In Baje there was a checkpoint so you couldn't move on to Han Bile. This part here was another entity, another unit which had no communication with the part below, with the Kljaci and the mine. Cukle, again, was encircled completely, and I'm not even counting it as a unit. They were completely isolated. But here again, from Han Bila and from Podovi, you could not go to Mehurici because in Podstinje and Puselje there were HVO checkpoints and you couldn't pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you sit down show us two points on the map, Ricice that you mentioned a couple of times, and Velika Bukovica. Where are they?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO is indicated in green and this territory is territory inhabited by Croats. They had HVO units and this circle indicates the village area of Ricice. Velika Bukovica, as you can see, the HVO positions were facing Vlasic. Velika Bukovica, or rather, Mala Bukovica is here. Radonjici is here and Velika Bukovica was cut because of from this Bosniak part on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down now. Please continue with your explanation of what led to the conflict which started a situation in which the brigade was fragmented and the population was under the blockade, as well as the command.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions I have just indicated, the territory, the village areas, the 306th Brigade as a brigade wasn't present in a sense; they didn't have a 1st battalion, a 2nd battalion, and 1st company, a 2nd company within the framework of those battalions. All those villages at the time of the conflict became battlefields in themselves and became units for themselves. So neither the company commander -- there wasn't a company commander but there was a village leader who was a sort of commander. And they would come to agreements among themselves with suggestions of those members of the brigades or those members of the battalions who happened to be there in the village. Because those are the instructions -- such are the instructions we gave them. So here we have Kljaci, Alihodze, Zukici, and Zolote, and part of Pirici near the Bila mine. That's one whole. The other whole the other entity would be Han Bila, Pode and part of the Brajkovici settlement inhabited by Bosniaks. And then another independent entity would be the village of Maline. They didn't have any links to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, I think this has already been explained to us. Could you tell us, in Krpeljici, did the command have its post there? What information did it receive from the field?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander and other members who happened to be there slept in two houses, two private houses. As I said, the command of the 2nd Battalion was there. But that battalion wasn't in one place because the representatives of the command from Maline couldn't come because in Mosor it was necessary to organise the defence of Mosor. So there were men in Mosor, too. So these were independent entities in a sense and they had a communications centre in a garage. And as part of the 306th we didn't have a command post that had been set up, but we just used the communications that the 2nd Battalion had in order to forward reports or cries for help to the mine, that is to say to the main command post. And they were to forward the information they received on from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you find out about the HVO attacks and the combat situation in the area you were in at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started addressing this issue. From that position it was possible to hear explosions and the fighting from the Lasva Valley. We didn't have any information as to what was happening but we sent instructions to the 3rd Corps command because we didn't have any links with the Bosanska Krajina or the Lasva OG. We sent reports to them asking information to know what was happening and we asked for assistance for the villages under threat, Ricice and the Velika Bukovica. We first received a report from the village of Ricice and they said they had been driven out of that village, I don't know how. But they weren't allowed to leave with their property. But there weren't any victims, fortunately. On the 4th of June in the afternoon or early evening we received a report from Velika Bukovica, according to which they were surrounded and they had received an ultimatum requesting they surrender and hand over their weapons. They refused to hand over their weapons and in the course of that day an attack was launched against Velika Bukovica. The brigade -- that wouldn't be a brigade command but it wouldn't have been humane for us not to try to help our subordinates, or rather the inhabitants of that village. The commander of the 2nd Battalion, since that was an area from which men were mobilised to enter the 2nd Battalion, was asked to send a unit to help Velika Bukovica. We received a report from him. He said that he wasn't in a position to comply with this request because the HVO was blocking the access route to Bukovica on the left-hand side. If you had a look at the map then you will see that the village of Radonjici is above the village of Krpeljici, whereas Mala Bukovica is in front of Velika Bukovica. So this area was under total control and it wasn't possible to send assistance from that direction. Later on we intervened in the direction of the forces in Mehurici. We requested that they intervene from Mehurici. We asked them to approach Bukovica and to provide assistance. The following day we received very alarming news. A report from Velika Bukovica, according to which there were 18 dead and six wounded. Such a small village; these enormous losses. We contacted the 3rd Corps command requesting they send UNPROFOR up there to help the civilians. There were civilians as well as soldiers. We did everything we could to do this but we didn't receive a response from UNPROFOR because I think they said at the time that they couldn't do this that it was necessary to inform the international monitors and it was only then that they would be able to do this to provide assistance. As far as this part of command is concerned when we managed to establish communications with Mehurici, we asked them to examine the situation in the field and try to provide assistance from any direction because the people in Velika Bukovica had to be helped. The only way to defend Velika Bukovica was to engage in active combat against certain HV positions in another area in order to improve the balance of forces in Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any available forces that were able to engage in combat so as to defend the positions of the 306th that had been attacked? What did you know about this? When did you find out about measures taken?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We insisted on something being done as soon as possible because the communications system was very poor. When you managed to get some form of communications, we could only use telegrams or be very brief because this was communications equipment from the former JNA and the HVO could have intercepted them. Because when we were preparing together, we had some sort of devices, I don't understand, from the maintenance department. But these were devices that could jam communications or intercept communications. But we asked the forces from Mehurici to intervene as soon as possible. We didn't know when they would intervene or if they would intervene. We were angry because there were cries for help from Bukovica all the time. And then on the 8th of June in the morning people started shooting all the time. We thought we were under attack. Commander Sipic asked this person from the command, from the main command post, to end him assistance because we were under attack from all directions. Why did we have such a feeling? It is because that morning the HVO attacked Bandol which is a village south of Krpeljici and Guca Gora. That is where we were located. And when attacking Bandol and probably since they knew part of the command was located in Krpeljici, the artillery was used to fire on Krpeljici. And one house in which we were located in or rather below which we were located in, as they say, when the shell fell it was destroyed completely. And then there was chaos. We didn't know who was attacking, we didn't know how. We thought we were under attack. Later on we discovered that while Bandol was being attacked forces from Mehurici set off to provide assistance to Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What direction did they set off in, since you said a minute ago that there was a report according to which they couldn't get through over Vrlete [phoen]? Which direction did they take, the direction towards Bukovica or towards other HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time I didn't know which direction was concerned then but later I found out that they went along the right bank of the Bila River towards Maline, Guca Gora, and towards Radonjici. The purpose was to reduce the front towards Velika Bukovica and to approach it, to take the elevated position called Hum above Radonjici and Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were the chief of staff, and as we can see in the documents from what you said, you constantly visited the field, the direction taken by your available forces towards Maline and Guca Gora from Mehurici, were those directions or areas in which the HVO had its own positions?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that in 1992 during the clashes in Novi Travnik, the open clashes in Novi Travnik, the HVO took certain positions facing Bosniak villages. And since before the clashes there was a joint operations team whose task was to go into the field, members of that team representing the 306th reported on the location of the HVO positions, which according to the joint order -- the order had to establish how the trenches would be filled in. There were trenches in all those areas and there were orders on combat action in the territory with Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, when you at the command post found out what your units from Mehurici were in fact engaged in, who did you find this out from and what sort of action did you take?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person who came to Krpeljici to our command, was the commander of the reconnaissance and antisabotage platoon of the 17th Krajina Brigade. I don't know his name but they called him Zenga [phoen], probably because he participated in the war in Croatia and it was customary to call the people who were in the war in Croatia like this. But he was the first one to appear. So pursuant to the decision from the joint command of the BH army and the HVO, it was decided that joint action should be planned against the Serbian and Montenegrin Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aggressor. And his platoon had already been forwarded to the Vlasic area in order to take action, together with the reconnaissance and sabotage platoon, to reconnoitre the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor and to provide information about their deployment, their possibilities, and to provide information about the joint action. So that platoon was in the area at the time in contact with Travnik in the Bila Valley. He was the first one to appear and he informed us that our forces had carried out an attack and that he had come to Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task after you had received that information?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander told me to go to the area above the village of Radonjici. That was my task. The area is called Sarici. I was to establish contact with the officers from the command who were in Mehurici, that is to say who had a mobile forward command post and were advancing their -- when I say a "mobile forward command post," this just means that these are ordinary people with Motorolas with batteries that were dead. So I was to go there to see how far men, our forces had reached. He could tell me what he had seen on his trip but we didn't have any further information. So I went there and in that area I met the assistant of the chief of staff for operations and training. And I asked for information about the positions reached by our forces. And he said that the forces had stopped, come to a halt, before Sarici. Because they were afraid it had been mined. He said they penetrated the HVO line at Simulje [phoen] and Maline. He said the lines had been penetrated there. He didn't have any information as to how far they had advanced after that. That was the information we received from him at the time. Then my further task was to establish contact, that is to say to climb the Hum hill which was above that position and there I was to establish contact with members of a company from the 4th Battalion, which was also participating in combat action in that area. This was to avoid mixing up units and misunderstandings with other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in your territory and given the cries for help you have mentioned, were there units who arrived from the wider area of the municipality, and at any point in time on that day or in the course of the following days, did you come into contact with other BH army units?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'll be mistaken as to the exact date. Whether it was on that day or on the 9th I don't know, but I met units of the 17th Krajina. Why? Because there was a problem. The units didn't have communications. They weren't linked up. The 17th didn't have any link with the 306th and our unit was on the Hum hill and my task was to go to see that unit again to see the 17th -- to receive the 17th who were coming from the positions facing the Serbian aggressor. So that battalion from the 17th took over the line that had been abandoned by the HVO. They sent that unit as assistance for Velika Bukovica. Because at that time we didn't have information as to what had happened to the civilian population in Velika Bukovica. Military-able men did penetrate from Obric and arrived in Mehurici. All the units arrived in Velika Bukovic. We didn't have any information about their fate. On that day it was very dodgy, as our people say, because the people from the Krajina Brigade didn't know us. But somehow we managed to establish contact and our joint task was then to go in the direction of Velika Bukovica. Our main task, as I said, was to take care of the civilian population Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the following days did you meet any other BH army units, and if you can remember that which units did you meet and when? And did you find out anything of what had happened to the population of Velika Bukovica and what had happened in the village of Bandol?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about this in chronological order. I can tell you when I met the units who broke out of Bukovica. There is no model here, but from Travnik, from the north and north-eastern side of Travnik you have a mountain or you have the Bukovica, which is about a 1.006 or 1.008 metres high. Travnik is about 500 or 540 metres above sea level. So it was difficult to climb up there. The units from Travnik, the first unit which appeared, was a mixed unit from the 312th and the MUP which was led from the staff of 312th Brigade, Zijad Sulejman, because I met him on that day. Since on that date he was killed. And that's why I remembered that date. Zijad Selman was from my village so we were neighbours and I remembered that. As far as other units were concerned, on the following day from Travnik via the road used by the 312th units, some of the units from the battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade used the same routes. They were engaged in Travnik Valley. I wasn't informed about this, though. I was concerned with the latest developments. And in further combat action, the unit of the 7th Muslim Brigade participated in combat -- in the attack towards Gostunj because Gostunj had not been liberated. And the Travnik-Guca Gora road could not be used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Siljak, I have two other questions for you. Firstly, when did part of the command meet for the first time and when did the command of the 306th meet at a whole?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems there is some mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think the transcript states -- after the witness said that he met the soldiers and officers from the 312th Brigade, one day later he met members of part of the 7th Brigade and that according to his information, because he had no information at the time, he said the unit was engaged in another area. I think the transcript is quite wrong. Line 18, page 29. Perhaps the witness could clarify this if, there is a problem with the transcript or with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it would be best if the witness told us when and where he met part of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said one day later, that is to say on the 12th, some of the units from the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade used the same route that had been used by the 312th, or a mixed unit from the 312th and MUP. This was over the Krpelj and Bukovica and that's the day which I met them because we were to jointly plan further combat action for these forces and that part of the 1st Battalion was participating in these forces in the direction of Gostunj. We were to plan further action in the direction of Gostunj. Gostunj is the first pass when you leave Travnik. On the map you can see the village of Bandol marked. So it is by the village of Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you for one answer before the break. What did you come across in Velika Bukovica and Bandol, and when did the command of your brigade meet?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Velika Bukovica -- I entered Velika Bukovica myself with the unit. Velika Bukovica had already been abandoned. Velika Bukovica and Mala Bukovica had been abandoned. And Velika Bukovica had been burned to the ground -- had been almost burned to the ground. There were no civilians there. And there was some bodies as a result of the combat and the units from Travnik had already taken those bodies away. They had arrived in Velika Bukovic before. So these units only searched the field because we didn't know what had been done before. We passed through Velika Bukovica and broke through to a feature in Bukovica, the mountain called Grahova Glava [phoen]. That's where we stopped on that day. As far as Bandol is concerned, from whichever direction you looked the situation was quite clear because Bandol, I don't know if there was a single house that hadn't been burned down in Bandol. The mosque in Bandol was completely destroyed. Later I found out that one man was burnt in his house. And the majority of the population nevertheless managed to flee together with the soldiers who were defending Bandol. They with drew towards the village of Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you first meet after that events with part of the command and when did the command meet as a whole?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this part of the command which wasn't really in function, we were in immediate contact, the chief of staff, the morale officer. But on the 12th, we had a meeting of other parts of the command, other members from the command who managed to come. And I would say that that was one of the first meeting of the core command of the 306th. And the command of the brigade from the 306th said that everyone should appear and that the command should start functioning as a whole in Krpeljici, not at the mine or anywhere else. They were to start functioning in Krpeljici. This was around the 20th. I'm not sure whether it was on the 19th or the 20th or the 21st, but it was in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that perhaps this is the right time for a break and after the break I will ask the witness what he knows about the Miletici, Maline, Guca Gora, and the measures taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you still require?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I said yesterday, we thought we would need six hours. I think that I used three hours and five minutes yesterday. And yesterday I managed to reduce my examination by half an hour. So I will need one hour at the most to conclude my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, when you were drawing the places yesterday with Bosniak and Croat population, you mentioned the Miletici village. Now please, do you know that in April 1993 -- or rather do you know what happened in April 1993 in Miletici? If you know, how did you find out? And tell us briefly exactly what you found out.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the events in Miletici village while I was in Daci [phoen], when I was ill. And to understand the whole picture, I'll tell you that we got orders from the command of the 3rd Corps that we should, together with parts of the 314th Brigade mount an attack on a feature from which HVO fired with artillery after the Ahmici attack. This feature is called Stozerak and it is at the border between Travnik and Vitez municipalities. From Stozerik, HVO fired with artillery weapons against villages in Vitez and Travnik municipality. Our order was to attack this feature. We did that on the 17th of April, a day after the Ahmici attack. Our task was successful. There were no losses on our side and we did not encounter a single corpse of HVO soldiers. And I suppose there were no losses on their side either because they were taken by surprise and they must have withdrawn from the feature earlier. However, earlier that evening I caught a cold and I got seriously ill with pneumonia later. And in one improvised infirmary I received injections, a series of 26 injections, two per day, while lying in a house nearby. Now, since that position on Stozerik was supposed to be secured by units of the 306th Brigade, the road from Han Bila to Stozerik passed by my house. And when going to those positions, members of the command, including a friend of mine Ribo Suljo who went to school with me and used to be a teacher with me in Mehurici told me what happened. What I heard was that the Mujahedin burst into the village and there was an incident within the village where one Croat from the village was killed, one of the Mujahedin was also killed. Later, they told me it was not a foreigner. It was a local man who joined the Mujahedin. I also learned that the entire population of Miletici village was taken by the Mujahedin to their base in Mehurici. I was specially interested in this because my assistant for intelligence affairs was from that village. They told me on that occasion that his father and his uncle had been tied down and taken together with all the other Croats to the Poljanice camp. My assistant of chief of staff for intelligence and Ribo Suljo took part in negotiations trying to persuade the Mujahedin to release the civilian population, and only after extensive attempts at persuasion, they managed to get the population released to Zagradje. But people were actually put up in the houses of Ribo Suljeman and his family to protect them, but that there were four Croats who were massacred by the Mujahedin. So the local population was taken captive by the Mujahedin, whereas these four Croats were killed, slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we go on, those Mujahedin you mentioned, are they the same about whom you told us that they transferred from the schoolhouse to Poljanice base?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that they are the same persons, but they are from the same group because there were frequent movements of this group and at a distance I didn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were ill at the time, but still you had some information. Tell me, did the 306th Brigade have any relationship of superiority over those Mujahedin located in that area?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither then or the entire duration of my stay with the 306th Brigade did our brigade have a superior position to the Mujahedin, had any control over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did anyone come to investigate what exactly happened in that village? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told then, maybe by some people who came to see me a couple of days later, that members of the international community and members of the joint commission came to see what happened. I know that General Merdan from the joint commission was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the joint command of the BH army and HVO. It was later called joint commission, later renamed joint command. And later he was part of the Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described in detail how the developments unfolded up to the first meeting of the joint command on the 12th of June. At that time or at any other time did you find out about some unfortunate events that happened during the combat on the 8th of June in the area where your brigade was active as well? If you did, what exactly did you learn?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in my testimony I tried to tell you what exactly my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. activities were at that time. My main job was combat activity and linkage with the forces in Velika Bukovica. Bandol village was on fire a bit further below. Another village to the south-east of Guca [as interpreted] was also under attack, Radojcici. The population and even the fighters from Radojcici withdrew in panic. My job was to insert forces from Vlasicici and link them up with the forces who were supposed to continue the combat action. I told you I met with my assistant for operations and training. At that time he was telling me about the operational aspect of the situation where exactly our forces were, but at that moment I didn't know anything untoward had happened. The first time I learned of any indications that that had happened was on the 12th when the inner circle of the command met, including the assistant commander for security. He said at that meeting that there were indications, in fact there is intelligence, that members of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade, while civilians and military-age population were taken away from Bandurici [phoen], the Mujahedin captured some Croats and at first nobody knew what happened with them. And later it was -- it transpired they were killed. However, on that day the assistant commander for security received orders to investigate who had done that. And I believe that in our regular operational report, we informed the command of the 3rd Corps of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although on several occasions you indicated that the assistant for intelligence or somebody else who was assisting the chief of staff was involved in this, tell me. The assistant for security, was he connected with the chief of staff and how did you find out what you found out after the orders came to investigate?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very title "assistant commander for security" speaks to the fact that he is not attached to the chief of staff. He is on the same level, and he directly reports to the brigade commander. It is the brigade commander who gives him assignments and the assistant commander for security is not duty-bound to inform the other members of the command of his own assignments. So what I was able to learn I was only able to learn during regular briefings if they were attended by a larger circle. Some parts of the report were fit for the larger circle and other parts would be only notified to the commander of the brigade, or maybe along the professional line to his superior commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of that system that was in place and that you just explained, do you know whether the security organs of the 306th Brigade did really investigate that prior information? And do you know took away those people from the column led by members of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it happened but the assistant commander for security, Delalic, reported at one of the briefings and issued an order to the assistant for security of the 1st Battalion to investigate, and the latter reported that while the column was moving towards Mehurici Croats were kidnapped by the Mujahedin accompanied by some masked people. Judging by the way they were speaking they were Arabs, and judging by their appearance, too. Together with them there were some more people wearing masks whom they couldn't recognise. At gun point they were separated from the group and taken away. No one knows where.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told me a second ago that they were never under the command of the 306th Brigade, I mean those foreigners who were based in Mehurici. Tell me now, did the 306th Brigade or any other organ of the BH army have authority or responsibility to investigate the conduct of individuals within other units, regardless of whether they were in their own area or not unless they belonged to your own brigade or to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you have such responsibilities or duties? And if not tell me to whom were you responsible.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had responsibility to investigate only the actions of our subordinates in our area, in the area from which we took reinforcement. There were members -- let me say just about the documents that we saw, there were illegal elements of the HVO. According to the decision of the presidency, the regular army did not include HVO. There were members of other brigades such as the 314th Brigade. There were members or elements of the 312th Brigade based there. As for people who did not belong to any of the brigades, we were not responsible. There were legal institutions of government, the local police in Mehurici, the judiciary outside the military structures. Therefore the assistant for security just reported that this was an incident that did not cause and did not involve members of our brigade. So further procedure would not be possible because we have neither the mandate nor the possibility to access that camp of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask another question. In fact, first of all, on page 38, line 7, you mentioned that there were illegal elements of the HVO, but you didn't come across as saying that you were not responsible for arresting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will either clarify this through the witness or I will ask that the transcript should record that the witness answered more fully than we can see from the transcript, from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this situation which you just described saying that there is a local police station in Mehurici, et cetera, et cetera. Tell me, do you know at all in keeping with the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina even before the war and for the duration of the war, which organs were duty-bound to deal with the issues of foreigners and their movements? Who received and who was tasked with gathering information on the identity of these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war I worked for the staff of the Territorial Defence, and in Travnik it was located in the same building as the public security station of Travnik. I know from that time that there was a special section dealing with foreigners in the public security station, or rather in the MUP. They dealt with all issues regarding the movement of foreigners, so that was not an issue that fell within the purview of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said a moment ago that these military age men, Croats, kidnapped and taken away from your unit were taken away, whereas when local civilians were being led towards Mehurici. Do you know why this civilian population was being taken from Maline to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very moment when this was happening, I had no idea it was going on. However, later from briefings, reports, and from my overall knowledge of the situation in the territory engulfed in combat action, I know that Maline was practically the foremost line of combat. And every unit was in charge of protecting its own civilian population. In this moment, the only possibility to protect civilians was to take them away from those localities. The only possibility in this case was to take them to the schoolhouse in Mehurici. From our experience from Miletici, we knew that they were informal armed groups, militants who were acting beyond the scope of any command. And there was a need to protect civilians because if they should stay in their homes, they would probably be targeted by those informal groups or Mujahedin. There were even demands -- I only heard about it. I can't say that I saw it myself -- that even the local population of Maline sought protection and wanted to be moved away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you first tell me briefly, did you personally visit the schoolhouse where they were put up and do you know what treatment they were subjected to, who guarded them, and who provided them with food?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not visit any schoolhouses and all I know I know from the briefings in the commander's office, from his assistants for logistics, security and security. And I learnt that they were in the gym of the schoolhouse in Mehurici, that they were guarded by the police station staff from Mehurici who, however, wanted reinforcement from the 306th Brigade because they were experiencing problems with the Mujahedin. Food was provided by the staff of civilian defence in Mehurici, relying on the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Already yesterday you mentioned those foreigners in your area and the problems they were causing to the army and the civilians. Today you said that at no point during your stay with the 306th Brigade were they subordinated to your brigade. Do you know whether your unit or any other unit of the BH army provided logistical support to these foreigners, the Mujahedin, in terms of weapons, equipment, food, or similar?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mujahedin only caused problems to us. There was no superior-subordinate relationship. There was no logistical support or any other support from the 306th Brigade, and I don't believe any other unit of our army provided it to them. However, I can only speak with certainty about my own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know or did the brigade command know who they are, what their names were? Did you have any precise information that would enable you to report in detail to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that anyone at any time had precise information about them. And to tell you the truth, we were not even interested. They were not within our field of competence. We did not seek information about them. We didn't know who they were or who their commanders were. They were not strictly established as a combat group. To me, they were some sort of passers-by that I avoided because all I could expect from them was inconvenience and embarrassment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your brigade ever issue any orders to those men and did it ever receive any reports from them?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the time that I spent with the 306th Brigade, I don't know that any orders had ever been issued to them or any reports had ever been received to them. And as far as orders are concerned, I should know in view of my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, in view of the fact that during those combat activities -- Krpeljici and Guca Gora are very close by. What is Guca Gora famous for?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an inhabitant of the municipality of Travnik. I live in Travnik and Guca Gora was always famous for the Guca Gora monastery. That's a symbol of Guca Gora. And I knew that they said that Guca Gora was the most progressive village in the Travnik municipality because the people there had the highest level of education, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you first tell me what the attitude of the Bosniak population was in the region around Guca Gora. What was their attitude towards religious buildings of other peoples and what sort of attitude and position did the 306th have -- what were their orders from the superior command? What had the 306th Brigade been ordered to do by the superior command in relation to religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders about how soldiers of the BH army should behave towards the population, towards prisoners, how they should treat religious buildings and the clergy, such orders started arriving from the corps command after the establishment. I don't know whether it was at the end of 1992 or perhaps at the beginning of 1993. That's when such orders started arriving. Then we had similar orders to regulate these matters in our subordinate units. In the field we tried to implement this through training. You showed me a document on which I commented on reports on training. The 3rd Corps command ordered that in order to train units, in order to turn them into soldiers, we should train these units. It wasn't possible to train entire units because units always had to be at their positions. So when certain units were available, we would carry out the training. I don't know which unit was in question here, but we could find out when the training was planned and when it was carried out. The brigade command planned the training. We would prepare battalion commanders. The battalion commanders would prepare or train their subordinate commanders, commanders of companies. The company commanders would train platoon and detachment commanders so that they could carry out training with their subordinates. Such training was implemented even before in the Territorial Defence and we proceeded on that basis then, too. So in the course of that training we also planned how to carry out -- how to respect the Geneva Conventions and international and humanitarian law. We wanted to familiarise these people with this, and this was a task for the assistant for morale in the brigade, too. Each brigade had an assistant for morale. In the company, there was also an assistant for morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just interrupt you there since you've mentioned this. When carrying out these orders from the Corps command, according to which it was necessary to train all the soldiers and all the commanding officers, in the framework of those programmes were there any foreigners, or rather Mujahedin, who participated in the training of your members?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I said who was involved in the organisation and implementation of the training and I mentioned how we trained men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of those orders, tell me do you know anything about the monastery in Guca Gora? Are you aware of it being damaged? Who damaged, if it was damaged? And do you know what the 306th or the 3rd Corps did and what measures it took, if any were taken?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this I was engaged in another axis [as interpreted] but I had information from the meeting on the 12th of June. And at that meeting I found out that a group of Mujahedin had broken into the monastery and they had destroyed its interior. I don't know what they did and how extensive the damage was. But they entered the monastery and the commander of the 306th sent his men to protect the monastery. I don't know on which day they managed to push the Mujahedin back from the monastery and members of the 306th, I don't know whether it was a detachment or a group of military policemen. They managed to provide security for the monastery. They managed to be present there.
